TRIGO MANPOWER BOARD · DESIGN REVIEW · 17 OCT 2026

Settings, redesigned four ways

Today's Settings page next to four directions, section by section, on desktop and on a phone. The proposals are live: open a row, toggle a day, change a permission, approve a request.

The “Today” frames are screenshots of the running app (1400×900 and 390×844) with sample data. Proposals use the same data, the app's navy and green, and its Geist font. Names, dates and counts are placeholders. In the screenshots the three engineers are not yet linked to accounts, which is why they read “— no account —”. Where a proposal shows a row of colour swatches, the build would keep the app's existing colour picker (16 presets plus a custom colour).

What is wrong today

Read from the code (index.html, styles.css, app.js) and from the screenshots below. Ten findings; each direction answers a different subset.

  • F1
    Every list is a grid of inputsEngineers, Service areas and Boards show every field as an editable box on every row. Nothing reads as content, and nothing says what is saved. Engineers · Areas · Boards
  • F2
    The explanation is told three timesA crumb, title and hint in the header, then a 2–3 line paragraph in the pane, then a footer reading “Changes apply when you save.” even when there is nothing to save. Every section
  • F3
    Roles is 76 dropdowns19 areas × 4 roles, each with a chevron. The Admin column is 19 greyed-out dropdowns for a role that cannot change. The grid reads as a form, not as a map of who can do what. Roles & permissions
  • F4
    One request, three placesA waiting request gets an amber banner, a “Review requests” filter, and Approve / Reject buttons at the far right of a seven-column row. Users
  • F5
    Users has two near-empty columnsLast seen and Requested show “—” for new accounts, the display name repeats beside the full name, and Email is the widest column. Users
  • F6
    “Where am I” and “what do I press” share a colourThe active rail item is a solid navy block, the same navy as every main button. Group labels are 10 px tracked capitals. Rail
  • F7
    Delete is always on screenEvery row carries an ✕ as heavy as the fields beside it. An area that still has employees cannot be deleted, but the row only says so after you try. Engineers · Areas · Boards
  • F8
    Boards reads backwardsTicked days are the days off, so the highlighted days are the ones nobody works. What the setting drives is explained in a paragraph, not shown. Boards
  • F9
    Desktop and phone disagreePhone: a section list, filter chips, one role at a time with Off / View / Edit. Desktop: tables and dropdowns. Same settings, two mental models. Users · Roles
  • F10
    Nothing says what needs doingTwo access requests are waiting, one engineer has no phone number, one area has nobody in it. You find out by opening each section. Opening screen

Four directions

They differ in how you move around Settings and how a page is built, not in colour. All four keep the app's palette, light mode and one navy for actions.

AQuiet rail

Keep the rail and the six sections; change how each page reads. People and areas become rows you open to edit. The save bar shows only when something changed. Users gets a waiting-for-access queue and Roles becomes a plain-word map.

Best for: lowest risk. Same sections, same ids, same panes.

BMaster–detail

Pick on the left, edit on the right. One real form per engineer, area, board, person or role, and a month preview for Boards. It is the phone's list-then-detail pattern, on a wide screen.

Best for: records with depth (people, roles). Heavy for three areas.

CTop tabs, one column

Drop the rail. Three tabs: My account, Board setup, People & access. Engineers, Service areas and Boards share one Board setup page, and the roles grid becomes an icon map that fits on one screen.

Best for: few clicks, wide tables. Biggest change to navigation.

DHub

Settings opens on a hub: what needs attention, then six tiles with live counts. Sections are cards, and a breadcrumb with a switch-section menu replaces the rail.

Best for: admins who open Settings to ask “what is pending?”

Today next to each direction

Choose a section once and all five rows follow. Clicking inside a frame moves only that frame. The rail items, tabs, tiles and rows all work.

How the four compare

My own judgement, not measurements. Effort and risk are against the current code: the rail, the #settings-tabs / data-tab / data-pane contract in app.js, and tests/e2e/settings-workspace.e2e.js.

A · Quiet railB · Master–detailC · Top tabsD · Hub
Removes the “wall of inputs” (F1, F3)●●●●Rows and plain-word cells●●●●One form at a time●●●●Compact rows, icon map●●●●Cards, role cards
Finding a setting●●●●Same rail, with counts and a badge●●●●Same rail, plus a list●●●●Three tabs, one scroll●●●●One extra click to enter a section
Tells you what needs doing (F4, F10)●●●●Queue card and rail badge●●●●Waiting sorts first●●●●Tab badge, pinned rows●●●●Attention strip on the hub
Roles readability (F3, F9)●●●●Map of all roles, click to edit●●●●One role at a time; matches phone●●●●All 19 areas on one screen●●●●Role cards plus list
Desktop / phone match (F9)●●●●●●●●Same drill-down●●●●●●●●Hub is the phone list
Build effortSmallCSS and row renderingMediumNew list/detail panes per sectionMedium–largeMerge three panes, new navMediumNew hub screen and menu
Risk to existing code and testsLowids and panes unchangedMediumPanes restructuredMedium–highRail and tab contract changeMediumRail replaced, panes kept

My pick

A as the base, with B's role editor and D's attention strip

A fixes the ten findings with the least movement: the rail, the six sections and the ids the code and tests rely on stay put. Two pieces are worth borrowing. B's one-role-at-a-time permission editor is already what the phone does, and it is the clearest answer to the 76-dropdown grid. D's “needs attention” strip is a cheap way to answer F10, and fits above A's My account page or as the Users queue.

Suggested order:

  1. Shell: quiet rail, one-line header, save bar that appears only with changes.
  2. Users: waiting-for-access queue, five columns, role chips.
  3. Roles: by-role editor on desktop and phone, Admin collapsed to a note.
  4. Engineers, Service areas, Boards as open-to-edit rows.

Choose C instead if Settings is used mostly by one admin on a wide screen and you are happy to retire the rail. Choose D if the main job of the page is triage.

Source: design/settings-redesign-directions.html. Nothing here is loaded by the app. Today's screenshots were taken from the running app with the end-to-end test harness and sample data; the proposals are static HTML with a little script.
